answer.label: Spoken by
answer.authorDates: b. 1997 · Pakistani education activist & Nobel Peace Prize laureate
answer.sourceLine: This is the closing line of Malala’s address to the United Nations Youth Assembly in New York on 12 July 2013 — her 16th birthday, and her first major speech after surviving being shot by the Taliban. The official Malala Fund transcript renders it “one child, one teacher, one pen and one book can change the world”; the popular form reorders it to “one book, one pen” and drops the “and.”

source.heading: The source

docMeta.dd: Address to the UN Youth Assembly
“…one pen and one book can change the world”

source.excerpt: So let us wage a global struggle against illiteracy, poverty and terrorism, and let us pick up our books and our pens. They are our most powerful weapons. One child, one teacher, one pen and one book can change the world. Education is the only solution. Education first.
trail: The line closes Malala’s UN Youth Assembly speech of 12 July 2013, published in full by the Malala Fund.
The independent Rev transcript renders the closing line in the book/pen order that the popular form uses: “One child, one teacher, one book, and one pen can change the world.”
Wikiquote’s sourced section confirms the line belongs to the UN speech and notes she reprised a reordered version at the Library of Birmingham inauguration.
She reprised the thought at the Library of Birmingham opening (Sept 2013): “even one book, one pen, one child and one teacher can change the world.”
source.excerptNote: The closing lines of the UN speech, per the Malala Fund transcript. The line that went viral reorders it to “one book, one pen” and trims the conjunction — a light drift in wording, not a fabrication.

author.name: Malala Yousafzai
author.heading: About Malala Yousafzai
author.metaLine: b. 1997 · Pakistani education activist · youngest-ever Nobel Peace Prize laureate
author.bio: Malala Yousafzai (born 1997 in Mingora, Pakistan) campaigned for girls’ education under Taliban rule in the Swat Valley and survived being shot in the head by a gunman in October 2012. Her recovery in Birmingham, England, and her subsequent activism made her a global symbol for education rights. In 2014, aged 17, she became the youngest person ever to receive the Nobel Peace Prize.

misattribution.heading: The credit is right — the wording drifted
misattribution.intro: Unlike most viral “inspirational” lines, this one really does belong to the person whose name is on it. The only thing that shifted is the exact wording as it was copied around.

items.why: In the UN speech — per the Malala Fund transcript — she said “one child, one teacher, one pen and one book can change the world.” The version that circulates on quote sites reorders it to “one book, one pen” and drops the “and.” Same meaning, lightly reworded.
She phrased the idea more than once. At the Library of Birmingham opening (Sept 2013) the order was “one book, one pen, one child and one teacher,” which is why several orderings float around online.

misattribution.truthLine: Bottom line: this is authentically Malala Yousafzai, from the close of her 12 July 2013 UN Youth Assembly speech — the popular wording reorders the words and trims one “and.”

context.heading: Why the line landed
lead: Malala delivered the speech at the UN on 12 July 2013 — her 16th birthday, nine months after Taliban gunmen shot her for advocating that girls attend school. The address, at what the UN dubbed “Malala Day,” was her first major public appearance since the attack.

The closing image — a child, a teacher, a book, a pen — distilled her whole argument into four everyday objects, framing education itself as the answer to “illiteracy, poverty and terrorism.” It is the sentence people remembered and reprinted.
context.pull: Let us pick up our books and our pens. They are our most powerful weapons.
